flashcards.tldr: Flashcards work for WSET because they force you to recall a fact instead of rereading it, and spaced repetition brings back the cards you miss sooner than the ones you know. Put one fact or one cause-and-effect link on each card (grapes, regions, label terms, key numbers) and review 10–15 minutes a day.
lead: Most of a WSET exam is recall under time pressure: which grape makes Barolo, what Kabinett means on a German label, how long a VSOP Cognac must age. Flashcards are the most efficient way to make those facts stick, provided you build them well and review them on a schedule rather than when you happen to remember. This page explains why they work, what belongs on a good card, how to organise a deck for each level, and the short daily routine that turns a pile of cards into marks on exam day.
body: Why do flashcards work so well for WSET exams?

Flashcards work because every review is a small test: you see a prompt, you try to recall the answer, then you check. That effort of retrieval is what strengthens memory, far more than reading the same page of notes again.

Learning research calls this the testing effect, and it pairs naturally with a second principle, spacing. A fact reviewed once a day for a week is remembered for longer than the same fact crammed ten times in one evening. Spaced repetition simply organises this: each card has its own interval, which grows every time you answer correctly and shrinks when you get it wrong.

WSET exams reward exactly the kind of knowledge flashcards build. Multiple-choice questions often hinge on one precise detail, such as a minimum ageing period or the grape behind a regional name, and the wrong options are designed to look familiar. If you have only recognised a fact while reading, a plausible distractor can fool you. If you have retrieved it twenty times from a blank prompt, it will not.
How spaced repetition decides what you see
In a spaced-repetition system, each answer moves the card along a ladder of intervals. A typical progression looks like this:
Card returns very soon, in the same session or the next day
Card returns after a short gap
Card is now long-term knowledge, reviewed rarely
The result is that your daily review time goes where it is needed: on the handful of facts you keep confusing, not on the ones you have known for weeks.
What should you put on a WSET flashcard?

Put one fact, or one cause-and-effect link, on each card, written as a question you can answer in a few seconds. Small cards are reviewed faster, failed more honestly and scheduled more precisely than big ones.
The syllabus for every level breaks down into a few families of facts. These are the ones that deserve cards:
Grape varieties: colour, typical aromas, and how the style changes from a cool to a warm climate (Chardonnay in Chablis versus Chardonnay in a warm Californian site).
Region and grape pairs: Sancerre and Sauvignon Blanc, Rioja and Tempranillo, Barossa Valley and Shiraz, Chianti and Sangiovese.
Label terms: Riserva, Crianza, Reserva, Kabinett, Spätlese, Brut, Extra Brut, Premier Cru, AOC/DOP, VS, VSOP, XO, reposado, añejo.
Key numbers: minimum ageing periods, minimum percentages of a raw material, exam-relevant temperatures for serving.
Processes and their effects: malolactic conversion, lees contact, carbonic maceration, pot versus column still, traditional versus tank method.
Food and wine interactions: what sweetness, umami, salt and acidity in food do to a wine.
For Level 3: causes and effects you will need in written answers, such as why a high diurnal range keeps acidity in the grapes.
Five rules for a good card
One answer per card. 'Name the three main grapes of Champagne' becomes three easier cards, or one card that asks for all three only once each grape is secure.
Ask in both directions for pairs. 'Barolo: which grape?' and 'Nebbiolo: name two famous wines' are two different memories.
Prefer 'why' to 'what' as you advance. 'Why is Mosel Riesling often light in alcohol?' trains the reasoning the exam wants.
Use the exam's vocabulary. Write 'pronounced', 'medium(+)', 'high acidity', not your own synonyms.
Add a short hook on the back: a map position, a contrast or a memorable example, so the answer has something to attach to.
Sample WSET flashcards for every level
The cards below show the right size and tone. Notice that each front can be answered in one breath and each back adds one useful link.
Pinot Noir. Chablis, also in Burgundy, is Chardonnay.
How does sweetness in food change a wine?
The wine tastes drier, more bitter and more acidic, and less fruity.
Serving temperature for a light-bodied red?
Kabinett on a German label means…
The lightest Prädikat level, made from grapes with the lowest minimum ripeness.
Traditional method: second fermentation in the bottle.
Sauvignon Blanc: intense, aromatic, high acidity.
Effect of a high diurnal range on grapes?
Cool nights slow the loss of acidity and help keep fresh fruit aromas.
Turns sharp malic acid into softer lactic acid; can add buttery notes.
Does Bourbon have to come from Kentucky?
No: anywhere in the USA, at least 51% corn, new charred oak.
Maple charcoal filtering before ageing (the Lincoln County Process).
Write the back as if explaining to a colleague in one sentence. If you need a paragraph, the card is too big: split it.
How should you organise a flashcard deck for each level?
Organise your deck by syllabus chapter, so you can study a topic the day you learn it, and let the spaced-repetition schedule mix the chapters back together over time.
The eight principal grapes, service temperatures, food and wine effects
Region–grape pairs, label terms, sparkling and fortified methods
Cause-and-effect links, regional detail, winemaking options, tasting terms
Raw materials, still types, the main categories and their label terms
Legal rules, ageing minimums, rum traditions, gin and liqueur families
These ranges are a guide, not a target. A smaller deck you review every day beats a huge deck you abandon in the third week.
Make cards the same day you learn

The best moment to create cards is straight after a lesson, while you still know what confused you. Five to ten new cards per study session is plenty. Adding forty in one go creates a review pile a few days later that feels impossible, and that is when most people stop.
Review the cards that are due every day, before adding new ones. Ten to fifteen minutes is enough for most learners, and consistency matters far more than session length.
Minutes 1–8: clear the cards due today. Answer out loud or in your head before turning the card, and be strict: a half-remembered answer counts as wrong.
Minutes 8–12: add five to ten new cards from the chapter you are studying.
Minutes 12–15: look at the cards you failed and ask why. Are two grapes or two regions blurring together? Make a contrast card that puts them side by side.
Once a week: take a set of practice questions on the same chapters to check that the flashcard knowledge transfers to exam-style questions.
Short gaps in the day are ideal: a commute, a coffee, the ten minutes before a class. Flashcards are the one study tool that works as well on a phone in a queue as at a desk.
Most flashcard problems come from cards that are too big, reviews that are too generous, or a deck that grows faster than you can review it.
Cards that hold a whole region. 'Bordeaux' as a front with ten lines on the back cannot be answered honestly. Split it into Left Bank grapes, Right Bank grapes, climate, key appellations.
Marking yourself right when you were close. The schedule only works if you are honest; a near miss should come back soon.
Only one direction. Knowing that Rioja is Tempranillo does not guarantee you can name a Spanish region for Tempranillo.
Skipping days, then bingeing. Missed reviews pile up; a short daily session keeps the queue small.
Using flashcards alone. Cards build facts; practice questions and mock exams test whether you can use them under exam conditions.

Flashcards are available for Wine Levels 1, 2 and 3 and for Spirits Levels 1 and 2, alongside lessons, practice questions with explanations, mock exams in the real format and short games. Because the cards follow the chapter order of each syllabus, you can study a lesson, review its cards the same day and then let the schedule bring them back in the weeks before the exam. The app is available in English, Italian, French and Spanish.
Pair every flashcard session with five practice questions on the same chapter. Cards build recall; questions check that you can spot the right answer among plausible distractors.

faq: Do flashcards really help for WSET exams?

Yes. WSET multiple-choice questions often turn on a single precise fact, such as a grape, a label term or an ageing minimum, and the wrong options are designed to look familiar. Flashcards train active recall of exactly those facts, and spaced repetition keeps them fresh until exam day. Combine them with practice questions so you also learn to handle distractors.
How many flashcards should I review each day?

Review all the cards that are due, then add five to ten new ones. For most learners this takes 10 to 15 minutes. If your due pile keeps growing beyond 20 minutes, stop adding new cards for a few days and let the queue settle. Daily consistency matters more than the number of cards.
What is spaced repetition?

Spaced repetition is a review schedule in which each card has its own interval. When you answer correctly the interval grows, so you see the card less often; when you miss it the interval shrinks and the card comes back soon. Your study time goes to the facts you are about to forget, not to the ones you already know well.
Should I make my own flashcards or use ready-made ones?

Both have value. Ready-made cards save time and follow the syllabus structure, so nothing important is left out. Writing a few of your own cards for the facts you personally keep confusing adds a second layer of memory. A good approach is to start from a ready-made deck and add contrast cards for your weak spots.
Are flashcards useful for WSET Level 3 written answers?

Yes, if you write cause-and-effect cards rather than single names. Cards such as 'Why does a high diurnal range help acidity?' rehearse the explanations the written questions reward. Flashcards will not replace practising full written answers, but they make the building blocks of those answers fast and reliable.
When should I start using flashcards before the exam?

From the first week of study. Spaced repetition needs time to work: a card first learned two days before the exam has had no chance to move into long-term memory. Start making cards as soon as you begin each chapter, so that by the final weeks you are reviewing, not learning facts for the first time.

planner.tldr: Start from your exam date, count the weeks you have, and split them into three phases: learn the syllabus, consolidate with practice questions, then revise with timed mock exams. A short daily goal (20–45 minutes depending on the level) beats long weekend sessions, and the last two weeks should be about mistakes and mocks, not new content.
lead: A good WSET study plan is not a long list of chapters: it is a calendar that works backwards from the exam date and tells you what to do today. This page shows how to build one, with weekly templates for Wine Levels 1, 2 and 3 (and notes for spirits), a sensible daily goal, the three phases of revision and a clear plan for the final two weeks.
body: How do you build a WSET study plan from your exam date?

Count the weeks between today and the exam, subtract one week as a buffer, and divide the rest into three phases: learning (about half), consolidation (about a third) and final revision (the remainder). Then turn each week into a short daily goal.

Working backwards protects you from the most common planning failure: spending too long on the first chapters and rushing the last ones. It also makes the workload visible. If you have 84 hours of study to fit into six weeks, you will see straight away that you need about two hours a day, and you can decide whether to start earlier or accept a lighter target.
Write down your exam date and your target grade (pass, merit or distinction where the level awards them).
Note the guideline study time for your level and the hours your course provides in class.
Count the weeks available and keep the last week free as a buffer for illness, work or a chapter that takes longer.
Assign chapters to the learning phase, roughly in syllabus order, with heavier chapters (regions, principal spirits) given more days.
Schedule one practice-question session per chapter and, from the consolidation phase on, one mock exam per week.
Convert the weekly load into a daily goal you can actually keep on a busy day.
50 multiple-choice + 4 short written answers, plus a blind tasting of 2 wines

The preparation windows above are practical suggestions, not rules. If your course is condensed into a few days, plan your private study around it: some before, to arrive familiar with the grapes and regions, and most after, between the course and the exam.
What daily goal should you set?
Set a daily goal you can meet on your worst day, then exceed it when you have time. For most people that means 15–20 minutes for Level 1, 30 minutes for Level 2 and 45–60 minutes for Level 3.

A daily goal works better than a weekly one because memory depends on frequency. Thirty minutes a day for six days gives you six rounds of retrieval; three hours on Sunday gives you one. A small goal also keeps your streak alive on hectic days, which matters more for motivation than it sounds.
Flashcards + one short lesson or 20 practice questions
Flashcards + lesson or questions + one written answer or tasting note
If you miss a day, do not double the next one. Simply meet the normal goal and move on; the plan has a buffer week for exactly this.
The three phases of WSET revision
Every good plan moves from learning new content, to using it in practice questions, to rehearsing the exam itself. The balance shifts as the date approaches.
Sign you are ready to move on
Lessons chapter by chapter, new flashcards, 10–20 questions after each chapter
Mixed practice questions, review of mistakes, contrast cards for confusions, first mock exam
Mixed-topic scores stable above the pass mark
Weekly or twice-weekly timed mocks, targeted revision of weak chapters
Mock scores comfortably above your target grade
Notice that practice questions start in the first phase, not at the end. Testing yourself straight after a lesson shows you what did not stick while the chapter is still fresh.
Weekly study templates for Wine Levels 1, 2 and 3
The templates below assume a typical preparation window for each level. Shift the weeks to fit your own date, but keep the proportions.
Types and styles of wine, the eight principal grapes, how wine is made in simple terms
Storage and service, food and wine pairing, tasting approach; two timed mock exams (30 questions, 45 min)
Tasting approach, factors affecting style (climate, winemaking), the eight principal grapes
France: Bordeaux, Burgundy, Loire, Rhône, Alsace; region–grape flashcards
Italy, Spain, Germany and other European regions; label terms
New World regions; sparkling and fortified wines; first mock exam
Mixed questions across all chapters; food pairing, storage and service; second mock
Final two mocks, mistake review, label terms and numbers; buffer days
The vineyard and winemaking in depth; Systematic Approach to Tasting; start a tasting note habit
France and Germany; one short written answer every other day
Italy, Spain, Portugal and the rest of Europe
New World regions; sparkling, sweet and fortified wines; first full mock
Mixed questions, written answers marked against key points, weekly mock, two tasting notes a week
Final mock, mistake review, light revision of weak regions; rest before the exam

For Level 3, written answers and tasting need their own slots from the start. They are assessed separately from the multiple-choice questions, and a strong score in one part cannot hide a weak tasting.

Spirits plans follow the same logic. For Level 1, one week on production and categories and one on tasting, service and cocktails is enough. For Level 2, give the principal spirits (whiskies, rum, agave spirits, fruit spirits, vodka) the largest share, since they make up almost half the exam, and do not neglect production, which accounts for more than a quarter of the questions.
How should you use the last two weeks before the exam?

Use the last two weeks to rehearse the exam and fix mistakes, not to learn new chapters. Two or three timed mock exams, a thorough review of every error and short daily flashcard sessions are the best use of this time.
Day 14 to day 8: one full mock under real timing, then spend the next two days on the chapters behind the mistakes. Repeat once.
Day 7 to day 3: a final mock, mixed practice questions on weak chapters only, flashcards every day.
Day 2: light review of label terms, numbers and your list of personal confusions. No new material.
Day 1: rest, check the exam time and location or online setup, sleep well. A tired brain loses more marks than one forgotten fact.
For Level 3: keep tasting until the end, writing full notes on every wine, but stop testing new regions in the last few days.
Most plans fail because they are too ambitious, too back-loaded or too passive.
Starting with long sessions and burning out by week three.
Reading every chapter before testing anything, so mistakes appear only at the end.
Giving every chapter the same time, although regions and principal spirits carry far more questions.
Leaving the first mock exam to the final week, when there is no time left to act on the result.
No buffer: one bad week and the whole calendar collapses.

faq: How long should I study for WSET Level 2?

The guideline is about 28 hours for Wine Level 2, including class time, and about 26 for Spirits Level 2. Spread over four to six weeks, that is roughly 30 minutes a day plus a few longer sessions for mock exams. Aiming above the 55% pass mark, around 70% in mocks, gives you a comfortable safety margin.
How long should I study for WSET Level 3?

The guideline total is about 84 hours for Wine Level 3, of which a large part is private study. Most people need ten to sixteen weeks at 45 to 60 minutes a day. Reserve regular time for short written answers and tasting notes from the start, because they are assessed separately from the multiple-choice questions.
Can I prepare for WSET Level 1 in a week?

Yes, for most people. Level 1 has a guideline of about six hours of study and a short exam of 30 multiple-choice questions in 45 minutes. A week of 20-minute sessions covering the principal grapes, service temperatures and food and wine pairing, followed by one or two timed mock exams, is usually enough.
When should I take my first mock exam?

Take your first full mock once you have covered most of the syllabus, around two thirds of the way through your plan. Doing it then leaves time to act on the result. Earlier, use shorter sets of practice questions after each chapter; later, take a timed mock every week until the exam.
What if I fall behind my study plan?

Do not try to catch up by doubling your daily goal. Keep the normal goal, use your buffer week, and cut low-value activities such as rereading notes. If you are still behind, shift time from the chapters you score well on to the ones you score poorly on. Moving the exam date is better than burning out.
Is it better to study every day or at weekends?

Every day, even briefly. Memory depends on how often you retrieve information, so six short sessions beat one long one of the same total length. Keep weekends for longer tasks such as mock exams, written answers or tastings, and use weekdays for flashcards, lessons and practice questions.

body: The Wine Goat is an exam-preparation and learning app for the WSET wine and spirits qualifications. It combines lessons, practice questions with explanations, flashcards, mock exams, games and a personal study plan in one place.

The app is independent: it is not run by WSET, it is not an exam body and it is not an Approved Programme Provider. You still enrol on your course and sit your exam with an approved provider. The Wine Goat is the place where you study and practise between classes and in the weeks before the exam.

How does it work, step by step?
You set three things once (level, exam date, target grade), and the app turns them into a daily routine. Everything else follows from that plan.
1. Choose your level, exam date and goal

Pick the qualification you are preparing, enter the date of your exam and choose the result you are aiming for: a pass, or a merit or distinction where the level awards them. If you are unsure which level to choose, the guides to each level compare the format, content and study hours.

The app spreads the chapters across the weeks you have and sets a daily goal. The goal reflects the time left and the grade you are aiming for. Each day you see what to do next, so you never lose ten minutes deciding.
3. Learn with lessons, questions and flashcards

Each chapter starts with a short lesson. Then you practise with multiple-choice questions: every answer comes with a short explanation and a deeper section on why the other options are wrong, which is where most learning happens. Flashcards with spaced repetition fix the key facts: grapes, regions, label terms and numbers.

Every question you get wrong goes into a review of your own mistakes, and the flashcards you miss return sooner than the ones you know. Instead of repeating what you already master, you spend time on the exact facts that keep tripping you up.

When you have covered most of the syllabus, the plan adds mock exams that mirror the real format and timing. Afterwards, every wrong answer joins your mistakes review, so you can see where marks were lost and go back to those lessons.

30 multiple-choice questions in 45 minutes, pass at 70%
50 multiple-choice questions in 60 minutes; pass 55%, merit 70%, distinction 85%
50 multiple-choice questions plus 4 short written answers
6. Keep a diary of what you taste

Point your phone at a label or a glass and the scanner adds the wine or spirit to your tasting diary, in 'My wines' or 'My spirits'. Linking what you study to what you actually drink is one of the most effective memory aids there is: the Rioja you had at dinner becomes a real example of Tempranillo, oak and ageing terms.
What tools are included, and what is each one for?
Each tool trains a different skill the exam needs: understanding, recall, recognition under pressure, timing and stamina.

Label and glass scanner, tasting diary
Whenever you open something worth remembering

Wine Level 3 adds tools for the parts of the exam that multiple-choice questions cannot cover: 101 open questions with model answers and marking points, so you can check your written answers against what earns marks, and a blind-tasting trainer built on the systematic approach to tasting. Maps, films and podcasts help with the regional detail.
Who is The Wine Goat for?
It is for anyone preparing a WSET wine or spirits exam who wants a clear daily routine and plenty of practice, whether you work in the trade or study for pleasure.
Beginners taking Level 1 or Level 2 who want to arrive at the exam calm and well practised.
Restaurant, bar, shop and wholesale staff fitting study around shifts, in ten- or twenty-minute sessions.
Level 3 candidates who need structure for a large syllabus, written-answer practice and tasting discipline.
Enthusiasts who simply want to learn wine or spirits properly, with or without an exam date.
Learners who prefer to study in Italian, French, English or Spanish (Spain and Argentina).
It is not a replacement for your course. Classes give you a tutor, guided tastings and the exam itself; the app gives you the practice and repetition between those sessions.
A typical day with the app
On a normal day, a Level 2 learner might spend about half an hour in short blocks rather than one long sitting.
Morning, 8 minutes: review the flashcards due today.
Lunch break, 10 minutes: read the next lesson in the plan, for example the Loire Valley.
Evening, 12 minutes: 20 practice questions on that chapter, reading the explanation for each mistake.
Weekend: one timed mock exam, then the mistakes review on the weakest chapters.
The daily goal is met, the streak continues, and the chapter progress bar moves. Over six weeks, that adds up to the guideline study time without a single marathon evening.
Can you study in your own language?
Yes. The app is available in Italian, French, English and Spanish, with separate versions for Spain and Argentina, so you can learn in the language you think in.

Many candidates study in one language and sit the exam in another, or take a course abroad. Being able to switch lets you understand a difficult concept, such as malolactic conversion or the solera system, in your own language first, then review the same chapter in the language of your exam so the key terms are familiar on the day. Reviewing in the exam language matters because the exam rewards precise terms rather than synonyms.
If your exam is in English but you study more easily in another language, learn each chapter in your language and do the practice questions and mock exams in English.
Common mistakes when studying with an app
An app makes practice easy, but it can also make it too comfortable. These habits keep it effective.
Rushing through questions without reading the explanations: the 'why the other options are wrong' section is where you learn the traps.
Repeating only favourite chapters because scores feel good there.
Skipping the mistakes review, so the same errors return on exam day.
Avoiding mock exams until the final week.
For Level 3, practising only multiple choice and neglecting written answers and tasting.

Wine Levels 1, 2 and 3 and Spirits Levels 1 and 2 are available today. Wine Level 1 and Spirits Level 1 are free. Spirits Level 3 and the Diploma are in preparation. Each available level includes lessons, practice questions with explanations, flashcards, mock exams, games and a personal study plan.

What happens to the questions I get wrong?

lead: These are the questions we hear most often from people preparing a WSET wine or spirits exam: which level to choose, how each exam works, how long to study, how to practise tasting, and how The Wine Goat app fits in. Each answer starts with the short version, then adds the detail that matters.
body: How many WSET wine and spirits levels are there?

Wine has four levels: Level 1, Level 2, Level 3 and the Level 4 Diploma. Spirits has three: Level 1, Level 2 and Level 3. Each level adds depth and a new kind of assessment. Levels 1 and 2 are tested with multiple-choice questions only, while Level 3 adds short written answers and a blind tasting, and the Diploma is a multi-unit programme for professionals.
Do I have to take Level 1 before Level 2?

No. Level 2, in both wine and spirits, is designed for people with little or no prior knowledge, so many learners start there. Level 1 is still a good choice if you want a gentle introduction or a quick certificate for a new job in hospitality. Level 3 is a different matter: Level 2 or equivalent knowledge is recommended before you enrol.
Which WSET level do I need to work in wine?

Level 2 is a solid foundation for restaurant service, retail and wholesale, because it covers the grapes, regions and label terms you meet every day. Level 3 is widely seen as the professional standard for buyers, sommeliers, educators and sales roles, since it trains you to explain why wines taste as they do. The Diploma is for those aiming at senior or expert positions.
Should I study wine or spirits first?

Start with the drinks you work with or enjoy most, because motivation and real-life examples make studying much easier. The two pathways are independent: you do not need a wine qualification to take a spirits course, or the reverse. Some topics overlap, such as tasting technique, oak and service, so the second pathway usually feels lighter once you have completed a level of the first.
What is the format of the WSET Level 1 exam?

Both Wine Level 1 and Spirits Level 1 are tested with 30 multiple-choice questions in 45 minutes. You need 70%, which means 21 correct answers, to pass, and there are no higher grades. Each question has four options and one correct answer. The pass mark is high because the questions are straightforward, so careless mistakes matter more than difficult ones.
What is the format of the WSET Level 2 exam?

Wine Level 2 and Spirits Level 2 each have 50 multiple-choice questions in 60 minutes. A pass needs 55% (28 correct answers), a merit 70% and a distinction 85%. Questions often test precise details such as label terms, minimum ageing periods or the grape behind a regional name, so a broad overview gives a pass while the higher grades need detail.
What is the format of the WSET Level 3 wine exam?

Wine Level 3 has two units. The theory paper combines 50 multiple-choice questions with 4 short written answers, and the tasting unit asks you to assess two wines blind using the Systematic Approach to Tasting. You need at least 55% in each unit, and a strong theory score cannot make up for a weak tasting. Higher results earn a merit or a distinction.
How long does it take to prepare for each level?

WSET's guideline study time, including class hours, is about 6 hours for Level 1, about 28 hours for Wine Level 2 (about 26 for Spirits Level 2) and about 84 hours for Level 3. In practice, most learners prepare Level 1 in one or two weeks, Level 2 in four to six weeks and Level 3 in ten to sixteen weeks of regular daily study.
Do wrong answers cost marks in the multiple-choice papers?

No. Each correct answer earns one mark and a wrong answer simply earns nothing, so you should never leave a question blank. If you are unsure, eliminate the options you know are wrong and choose among the rest. Practising with timed questions helps you manage this calmly: at Level 2 you have about 72 seconds per question, which is usually enough.
What is the best way to prepare for a WSET exam?

Use active methods rather than rereading. Learn each chapter, then test yourself straight away with practice questions; build key facts into flashcards reviewed with spaced repetition; review every mistake; and take timed mock exams in the final weeks. Short daily sessions work better than long weekend ones. For Level 3, practise written answers and tasting notes from the very start.
How can I practise blind tasting for Level 3?

Taste regularly and write a full note on every wine using the Systematic Approach to Tasting: appearance, nose, palate and conclusions on quality. Use the exam's exact terms, because synonyms do not score. Ask someone to pour wines for you without showing the bottle, compare classic styles side by side, and justify quality with balance, length, intensity and complexity.
Are practice questions online the same as the real exam questions?

No. Real exam papers are confidential, and no app or website can offer them. Good practice questions, like those in The Wine Goat, are written to reflect the published syllabus and the exam format, so they train the same knowledge and the same skill of choosing between plausible options. Treat them as training, not as a preview of your paper.
How many mock exams should I take?

Two to four full mocks is a good target for Level 2, and at least three for Level 3, spread over the final third of your preparation. Take the first one early enough to act on the result. Run each mock under real conditions, with the timer on and no notes, then spend more time reviewing your mistakes than you spent on the mock itself.
Is The Wine Goat affiliated with WSET?

No. The Wine Goat is an independent exam-preparation app. It is not affiliated with, endorsed or sponsored by the Wine & Spirit Education Trust, and it is not an Approved Programme Provider or an exam body. You enrol and sit your exam with an approved course provider, and use The Wine Goat to study, practise and revise alongside your course.
Which levels does the app cover?

Wine Level 1, Wine Level 2 (about 1,070 practice questions), Wine Level 3 (more than 2,000 questions, 101 open questions with model answers, a blind-tasting trainer, maps, films and podcasts), Spirits Level 1 (about 210 questions) and Spirits Level 2 (about 1,000 questions). Spirits Level 3 and the Diploma are in preparation and will be added when ready.

Yes. Wine Level 1 and Spirits Level 1 are free, with lessons, practice questions, flashcards, mock exams and games, and you can try the other levels free too. Starting with a free level is a simple way to see how the study plan, the explanations and the spaced-repetition flashcards work before you focus on your main exam.
In which languages is the app available?

The Wine Goat is available in Italian, French, English and Spanish, with separate versions for Spain and Argentina. You can switch language, which is useful if you study more easily in one language but sit the exam in another: learn a difficult chapter in your own language, then review it in the exam language so the key terms feel familiar.
Which devices can I use, and does it work offline?

The Wine Goat runs in the browser on phones, tablets and computers, and you can add it to your home screen like a regular app. Once it has loaded, much of the app keeps working without a connection, which is handy on a train or plane. Podcasts and films stream, so they need a connection, and your progress syncs when you are back online.
What data does the app keep about me?

The app keeps what it needs to run your study: your account details, your chosen level, exam date and target grade, your answers, progress and streak, and the entries you add to your tasting diary. This is what lets your plan adapt and your mistakes come back. You can contact The Wine Goat to ask about, correct or delete your data.
Does WSET or my course provider see my results in the app?

No. Because The Wine Goat is independent, your practice scores, mock exam results and mistakes stay in your own account and are not sent to WSET or to your course provider. Your official result comes only from the exam you sit with your approved provider. Mock scores in the app are a guide to your readiness, not a prediction of your grade.
